outcome: I can connect a complex argument while making concessions and limits explicit.
explanation: Cohesion is the way a text's parts connect so a reader can follow the reasoning. Encore faut-il que (provided also that/it still remains necessary that) introduces a condition that qualifies an apparent solution and takes subjunctive. Cela étant (that being said) returns to the main argument after a concession; dès lors (from that point/therefore) can signal a consequence, depending on context. A formal concessive pattern, si + adjective + subjunctive (Si utile soit-elle… — useful though it may be…), concedes a quality before limiting its effect. Do not mistake stylistic variety for logical precision: identify whether you add evidence, concede a point, impose a condition or infer a result before choosing a connector.

outcome: I can report a complex claim without losing attribution, timing or uncertainty.
explanation: Reporting a message requires tracking who asserts it, when it applies and how certain it is. Selon (according to) and d'après (on the basis of/according to) attribute a claim; aurait plus a participle can distance the reporter from unconfirmed information. Do not turn an allegation into a fact by dropping those markers. Past reporting can place an earlier action in plus-que-parfait and a later action in conditional; indirect questions retain statement order. A tense can remain unchanged when the current narrator explicitly endorses a still-valid fact, so explain the viewpoint rather than applying a mechanical shift.

feedback.rule: Reporting a message requires tracking who asserts it, when it applies and how certain it is. Selon (according to) and d'après (on the basis of/according to) attribute a claim; aurait plus a participle can distance the reporter from unconfirmed information. Do not turn an allegation into a fact by dropping those markers. Past reporting can place an earlier action in plus-que-parfait and a later action in conditional; indirect questions retain statement order. A tense can remain unchanged when the current narrator explicitly endorses a still-valid fact, so explain the viewpoint rather than applying a mechanical shift.

outcome: I can shift between familiar and formal language while preserving the request.
explanation: Register concerns audience, relationship and setting, not simply difficult vocabulary. Colloquial speech may use ça (that/it), shortened negatives and familiar requests; neutral language works across many contexts; formal or academic language tends toward explicit relationships and careful qualification. Rewriting should preserve the requested action and interpersonal stance, not add unnecessary abstraction. A contraction appropriate in conversation can be distracting in a report, while a ceremonial formula may sound distant among close colleagues. Regional and organizational norms also matter.

outcome: I can build a persuasive argument that fairly addresses a strong objection.
explanation: Advanced persuasion combines credible support, explicit reasoning and an understanding of the audience's priorities. Distinguish correlation (two things occurring together) from causation (one producing the other). Rhetorical questions may guide attention, but they do not replace evidence. End with an action or conclusion proportionate to what your reasoning establishes.

outcome: I can separate an explicit statement from an implied stance and justify an inference.
explanation: An inference is an interpretation supported by clues rather than directly stated. Presuppositions are ideas treated as already given: encore in il est encore en retard (he is late again) implies an earlier occurrence. Irony can make literal praise convey criticism, but context and tone are essential; words alone may leave several plausible readings. Identify the explicit message first, cite a specific clue for the implied stance, and preserve uncertainty where evidence is weak. Have a partner read the mini-text twice with different intonation to test how tone changes interpretation.

outcome: I can interpret an idiom in context and choose when to use or paraphrase it.
explanation: An idiom is a conventional expression whose overall meaning may differ from the literal words. Mettre de l'eau dans son vin literally means put water in one's wine, but means moderate one's demands. Jeter l'éponge (throw in the towel) means give up. Avoir le vent en poupe (have the wind at one's stern) means enjoy favourable momentum. Figurative language can create familiarity or vividness but may confuse an unfamiliar audience. Avoid assuming an expression is equally common or appropriate across regions and professional settings.

explanation: Critical reading examines not only what a text claims but how it guides interpretation. Framing selects which aspect becomes central; charged words can present a judgement as a description. Distinguish an author's direct claim from a quoted source and check whether the evidence actually supports the conclusion. Bias is a pattern in selection or presentation, not simply a view you dislike. In your analysis, cite a specific language choice and explain its effect; do not infer hidden motives without evidence. The mini-text is an original invented editorial example, not an authentic news quotation.

outcome: I can negotiate a complex disagreement and reformulate spontaneously.
explanation: Advanced speaking requires responding to what was just said while keeping a coherent position. Reformulation restates a point in new words to clarify it: si je vous suis bien (if I follow you correctly). A negotiation distinguishes shared objectives from competing constraints and tests a proposal against both. Use a pause or a brief framing phrase to organize a response, rather than filling time with unsupported assertions. Precision includes correcting your own wording when it overstates your position.
